chapters.title: Why it really ended (your side of it)
chapters.teaser: Not who was right. What your soul was doing while it fell apart.

chapters.title: Your breakup pattern
chapters.teaser: How you end things, how you grieve, and the habit that slows you down.

chapters.title: Why you keep checking
chapters.teaser: What the pull back toward them is really asking for.

chapters.title: So, will they come back? The honest answer
chapters.teaser: What a chart can and can't tell you, and the question that matters more.

chapters.title: If they ever reach out
chapters.teaser: Three questions to ask before you reply, built for your soul.

chapters.title: What you do now
chapters.teaser: The next small steps that help, whatever they decide.

text.why-it-ended: Gye Water is the rain, the mist, the quiet water that gets into everything. You're intuitive and gentle, and you feel the mood of a room before anyone speaks. In your last relationship you probably sensed every shift and adjusted yourself to soothe it. Rain doesn't always announce itself. You may have kept your real feelings vague, hoping they'd guess. Partners often love the mystery at first and then struggle with never quite knowing where they stand. Look at the gap between what you felt and what you actually said. That gap is where most of this story lives.
text.your-breakup-pattern: You grieve softly and privately. Gye Water absorbs feelings, yours and theirs, so you may be carrying their sadness along with your own. Your pattern is retreating into imagination: alternate endings, imagined conversations, songs that fit a little too perfectly. That inner world comforts you, and it can also keep the wound fresh. You might blur the ending too, staying vaguely in touch so it never fully closes. Clarity is a kindness, including to yourself. A clean, gentle ending heals faster than a soft one that never quite finishes. You deserve an ending you can actually walk away from.
text.the-pull: What pulls you back is the emotional bond, the sense that you understood each other without words. Gye Water forms almost wordless connections, and losing one feels like losing a language only two people spoke. That's real grief. But notice whether the connection lives more vividly in your memory now than it did in the actual relationship. Rain makes everything look softer. Write down what was really said and done, the good and the hard. Then hold the real version next to the dreamy one and see which one you're missing.
text.the-honest-answer: No chart can read what another person will choose, and we won't pretend yours can. What we can see is your sensitivity, and your habit of letting people guess. If you hope they'll come back, ask what you would say differently. Would you name your needs clearly? Would you speak up when something hurt, instead of weeks later or never? Gye Water's love is deep, and it deserves to be seen. Whether with them or someone else, the honest work is saying more of what you feel, out loud, in actual words.
text.if-they-reach-out: If they reach out, you'll sense the mood of the message instantly and probably start adjusting to match it. Try not to. Before replying, work out what you feel, separately from what they seem to feel. Gye Water mirrors very easily. Then write one clear sentence about where you stand. It can be warm. It should be clear. If you'd like to reconnect, suggest a real conversation instead of endless late-night texting. If not, a gentle, specific goodbye is kinder to both of you than slowly fading out. Clear is not the same as cold.
text.what-you-do-now: Give your feelings a riverbank. Gye Water flows everywhere unless it has a shape. Try a simple routine: a walk at the same time each day, a few lines in a journal before bed, one friend you call every week. Make art if it's calling you, music, writing, drawing, anything. Spend time near real water. And practise saying small preferences clearly, where to eat, which film to watch. Every clear little sentence builds the muscle for the big ones. You're not too much and you're not too quiet. You're ready to be heard.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You felt everything they felt, Gye. That's a rare gift.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Then you hoped they'd guess your feelings. They didn't. They never do.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Your inner world is comforting. Visit, don't move in.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Write down what really happened. Not the version with rain effects.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: One clear sentence. Warm, but clear.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Fading out isn't a goodbye. Say the actual words.

spring.intro: Spring rain, Gye, is the gentle kind that makes everything grow. Wood ruled your birth season and Water feeds Wood, so your care flows out softly: noticing, listening, quietly helping someone bloom. In the relationship you probably gave more emotional support than anyone saw. The breakup may have left you feeling invisible, like the rain nobody thanks for the flowers. That's where the checking comes from. You want to see whether what you poured in still shows. It does, in them and in you. Spring Gye needs to remember that rain can fall on its own garden too. Turn the attention you gave them inward for a while.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Nobody thanks the rain, Gye. I'm thanking you. Now rain on yourself.

summer.intro: A summer shower vanishes on hot pavement. Fire ruled your season, Gye, and Water controls Fire, so you were born handling a lot of heat with very little water. In love you probably tried to cool things down, soothe their temper, keep the peace. It's exhausting work for a small cloud. After the breakup you may feel wrung out and unusually foggy. Summer Gye sometimes stays attached because the relationship was the most intense weather you'd felt, and calm skies seem empty by comparison. Calm is not empty. It's recovery. Let your reserves refill with Metal: structure, clear routines, people who are reliable rather than thrilling.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Calm feels boring because you got used to storms. Boring is healing, babe.

autumn.intro: Autumn mist rises off cold stone, Gye. Metal ruled your birth season and Metal generates Water, so your intuition is well fed and unusually sharp. You probably saw the end coming before anyone said it, maybe before they knew it themselves. That clarity doesn't make it hurt less. It makes it hurt earlier and longer. After the breakup you might be replaying signs you noticed and ignored. Be gentle about that. Seeing something and being ready to act on it are two separate skills. Autumn Gye's blind spot is living in the knowing instead of the doing. The pull back is your intuition still talking. Thank it, then give it a new subject.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You saw it coming months ago. Knowing early isn't the same as failing.

winter.intro: Winter Gye is snow, Water at its quietest and fullest. The season doubled your element, so you feel deeply, imagine vividly and keep most of it to yourself. In love you probably built an entire inner world around the person, rich and private. After the breakup, that world is still standing, fully furnished, and you visit it at night. That's the pull. It isn't really about whether they'd return. It's that the imagined version is so detailed it feels like somewhere you live. Winter Water needs warmth and earth: sunlight, a body moving, something solid in your hands. Snow melts into spring. You won't stay frozen in this.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: That inner world is beautiful, Gye. Visit by day, not every night.

strength.strong: Your chart feeds your rain with plenty of Water and Metal, Gye, so your intuition and inner life are huge. In love you sense everything, including things the other person never said. In a breakup that can become certainty about their thoughts, their reasons, their feelings. You might be building full theories about what they meant. The blind spot is that strong intuition can drown out what people actually tell you. Ask whether your version of them is the real one or the one you imagined. Mist is lovely. Clear air shows the path.
strength.weak: With thin support around your Day Master, Gye, you can evaporate in a strong partner's heat. In love you probably gave quietly and needed loudly, without ever saying so. You picked up their moods and set aside yours. After the breakup you may feel like there's barely anything left of you. There is. Rain gathers again. Be with people who notice when you go quiet, and say one need out loud this week, even a tiny one. Your softness isn't the problem. Being unheard was.

balance_text.too_much_wood: Too much Wood means you push for growth and answers, even in heartbreak. You want a plan for getting over it, maybe even a plan for getting them back. Slow down. Not everything grows on schedule, and some things need to just sit for a while. Ask for help instead of turning healing into a project. For balance, let a little Metal in: declutter, finish old things, clear out the drafts folder. A clean edge helps Wood stop reaching for what's already gone.
balance_text.missing_wood: Missing Wood means fresh starts feel heavy. After a breakup you might stay in the same place, emotionally and literally, for longer than you'd like. That isn't weakness. It just means new growth needs a nudge. Small steps work best: a new route to work, one new class, one new person a week. Get outside in the mornings and keep something green near you. You don't need a whole new life. You need one new branch, and then another.
balance_text.too_much_fire: Too much Fire makes you feel everything at full volume. A breakup can feel like an emergency, with urges to text, post, or fix it all tonight. Your passion is real, but heat isn't a strategy. Before any big move, sleep on it. Cool down with water: swimming, long showers, quiet evenings at home. Talk to your calmest friend before your most exciting one. Let the fire warm you instead of burning through your peace.
balance_text.missing_fire: Missing Fire means joy and visibility don't come easily, and after a breakup you might go dim for a while, hiding from people and from fun. Turn the lights back on gently. Sunshine, music, dancing in the kitchen, one social plan a week even when you'd rather stay in. Letting people see you is the medicine here. Warmth doesn't only live in romance. It's in friends, in laughter, in simply being out in the world.
balance_text.too_much_earth: Too much Earth means you hold on: to routines, to memories, to the hope that things will settle back into their old place. Stability is your gift, but in heartbreak it can turn into staying stuck. Shake the ground a little. Move the furniture, take a short trip, try something unplanned. Let some Wood energy in, growth and new beginnings. You can keep what was good and still leave room for something new to grow.
balance_text.missing_earth: Missing Earth means life can feel unsteady, and a breakup can knock away what little ground you had. You might feel scattered, unsure where to put your feet. Build structure gently: regular meals, a steady bedtime, one place at home that's only yours. Cook something. Walk somewhere. Lean on the people who are reliable. Stability first, big decisions later. You need solid ground under you before deciding anything about the past.
balance_text.too_much_metal: Too much Metal makes you sharp and decisive, sometimes too quickly. You may have cut the relationship off cleanly and then refused to look at what you feel. Or you judge yourself harshly for every mistake you made in it. Soften the edges. Let Water in: rest, tears, music, journaling. Feeling the grief isn't the same as reopening the door. You can keep your boundaries firm and still let your heart thaw.
balance_text.missing_metal: Missing Metal means boundaries are hard, so after a breakup you might keep the door half open, answer every message, or stay friends when it hurts. Practise clean edges. Mute without guilt. Box up their things. Say no without explaining. White and silver, tidy spaces and finished tasks all help your chart. A boundary isn't cold. It's how you protect the part of you that's still healing.
balance_text.too_much_water: Too much Water means you think and feel deeply, maybe endlessly. After a breakup you might drift through memories, analyse every detail, and lose sleep to what-ifs. Your intuition is a gift, but it needs riverbanks. Add some Earth: routines, cooking, walks, people who ground you. Give overthinking a time limit. Feel it fully, then get up and do one ordinary thing.
balance_text.missing_water: Missing Water means rest and reflection get skipped. You may rush past the breakup, staying busy so you never have to sit with it. That works until suddenly it doesn't. Build in quiet on purpose: slow mornings, water by your bed, a few lines in a journal at night, a bath instead of another plan. Let yourself feel without fixing. Intuition grows when you give it some silence.

too_much_wood.speaker: yeon
too_much_wood.text: So much Wood. You've drafted three versions of 'hey, random but' already.

too_much_wood.speaker: bom
too_much_wood.text: That growing energy wants a goal. Give it your own plans, not their inbox.

too_much_fire.speaker: yeon
too_much_fire.text: Too much Fire: every feeling is a five-alarm emergency. It's a breakup, not an inferno.

too_much_fire.speaker: bom
too_much_fire.text: Your passion is beautiful. Let it cool before you hit send on anything.

too_much_earth.speaker: yeon
too_much_earth.text: Heavy Earth. You'd still be in that relationship purely out of habit.

too_much_earth.speaker: bom
too_much_earth.text: Your loyalty is rare. Just make sure you're loyal to yourself too.

too_much_metal.speaker: yeon
too_much_metal.text: Lots of Metal. You cut them off cleanly, then reread everything at midnight.

too_much_metal.speaker: bom
too_much_metal.text: Being firm protected you. Being gentle with yourself will heal you.

too_much_water.speaker: yeon
too_much_water.text: Overflowing Water: you've cried to three songs and written a novel in your notes app.

too_much_water.speaker: bom
too_much_water.text: Feeling deeply is a gift. Just come up for air sometimes.

missing_wood.speaker: bom
missing_wood.text: Missing Wood can make moving on feel stuck. Small new routines count as growth.

missing_wood.speaker: yeon
missing_wood.text: You haven't changed anything since the breakup, including your lock screen. Start there.

missing_fire.speaker: bom
missing_fire.text: Missing Fire can make joy feel far away. Borrow some from a loud friend.

missing_fire.speaker: yeon
missing_fire.text: You stopped having fun when they left. Fun was never theirs to take.

missing_earth.speaker: bom
missing_earth.text: Missing Earth can make everything feel unsteady. Simple routines will hold you.

missing_earth.speaker: yeon
missing_earth.text: No Earth, no anchor. You re-decide whether to text them every hour.

missing_metal.speaker: bom
missing_metal.text: Missing Metal makes boundaries tricky. You're allowed to say no to your own phone.

missing_metal.speaker: yeon
missing_metal.text: No Metal means you'll answer at 2am. Put the phone in another room.

missing_water.speaker: bom
missing_water.text: Missing Water can make grief hide. It's okay to let it surface slowly.

missing_water.speaker: yeon
missing_water.text: You said you're fine twelve times today. Water would like a word.

gap-wood.title: Morning rain on the oak
gap-wood.text: You loved a tree and spent a lot of time being misunderstood by it. Your Gap Wood ex was steady, protective, direct. You sent the song that said everything; they replied 'cool, is dinner still at 8?' You hinted at what was bothering you; they asked you to just say it, and then, when you went quiet, they asked again, louder. You felt interrogated. They felt shut out. And underneath, you were soaking up their stress like rain into soil, quietly, without saying how heavy it was getting, until you couldn't anymore. The hurt has a clear outline: you gave care they never saw, because you never named it, and they gave care you couldn't feel, because it came as plans and questions. The pull is their solidity. When your feelings were weather, they were a fixed point. Practise saying the thing you'd normally hint at, in one plain sentence. 'I'm upset you forgot.' 'I need a quiet evening.' Then send the song. Clarity first, poetry after. You'll be surprised how much lighter that feels.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, the moon screenshot was lovely. The sentence under it would've been lovelier.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, you asked 'what's wrong' like a police officer. Try 'I'm here' instead.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Rain and an oak are a good pair. They just needed subtitles.

eul-wood.title: Dew on the petals, wished away
eul-wood.text: You loved a vine who tried, endlessly, to cheer you up. Your Eul Wood ex sent the funny video, the plan for Saturday, the 'let's get out of the house', and when your mood didn't lift, they took it personally. You withdrew, because that's how rain processes things. They felt rejected and didn't say so. You felt pressured to be fine and didn't say so either. Two people who hate conflict can be very gentle and very lonely in the same flat. Neither of you set direction, so plans dissolved, practical things went unattended, and one day the whole thing felt unworkable without either of you able to name a single fight. You were truly kind to each other, and that makes it harder, not easier. What tugs is how they kept trying. Tell people what helps you when you're low. 'I don't need cheering up, I need company.' One sentence like that, said early, saves the other person from guessing and saves you from being guessed at.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, they tried so hard to make you smile. Tell people what actually helps.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Eul, you can't sunshine your way out of somebody's weather.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Say the hard thing clearly. Then add the song.

byeong-fire.title: Sunshine and drizzle
byeong-fire.text: You were the drizzle and they were the sunshine, and when you met there were rainbows. Your Byeong Fire ex was warm, loud, constantly reaching for you with messages and voice notes and plans. You replied slowly, thoughtfully, sometimes not at all, because that's how you process. They took your quiet as disinterest. Their bluntness landed on you as carelessness, and their jokes during tense moments made you feel your feelings were being waved away. So you withdrew, and they pushed, and the weather got heavy. You felt too much and too quiet at once, always a little out of step with their brightness. Their light is what tugs. They made grey days easier, even when you didn't say so. Send the small signal. A heart, a 'still here, just quiet today'. It costs you little and tells loud, warm people that your silence isn't a closed door. You can keep your depths and still leave the porch light on.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, 'still here, just quiet' is a whole love letter to a sun.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Byeong, joking through their sadness isn't comforting. It's dodging.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Rainbows need both. That part was true.

jeong-fire.title: Rain on the candle
jeong-fire.text: You were the rain and they were the candle, and the closeness was both beautiful and a little dangerous for the flame. Your Jeong Fire ex wanted to know what you were feeling, clearly and often. You needed room to not know yet. When they asked, it felt like being searched. When you went quiet, it triggered their anxiety, and they asked more. Your moods could dim them, and you knew it, which made you feel guilty, which made you quieter still. Both of you withdrew when hurt. Conflicts didn't explode; they just went silent and stayed there. Being loved for your depth and then pressured for it is the wound. Their warmth is what you miss. They noticed you, really noticed, and few people do. Offer a small piece of clarity before it's requested. 'I'm in a low mood, it's not about you.' That one sentence protects your privacy and their peace at once. Silence is allowed. Silence as punishment, on either side, never was.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, 'it's not about you' is the kindest sentence for a worried candle.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, asking 'what's wrong' four times is not support.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Silence is allowed. Just not as a weapon.

mu-earth.title: Mist on the mountain
mu-earth.text: Mist on a mountain: that's what you two were, a Heavenly Combination, softness wrapped around something solid. Your Mu Earth ex gave you ground when your feelings were weather. But you shared your heart in poems and moods and long messages at night, and they replied with solutions. 'Maybe go for a walk.' 'Have you eaten?' You felt dismissed. They felt confused, because they were trying to help. Your changes of mood unsettled them; their steadiness sometimes looked like they didn't feel anything at all. And their instinct to organise your life made you feel contained, like mist in a jar. Feeling unmet by someone who never left is the particular grief here. The steadiness is what you miss. With them, you had somewhere to land. Appreciate practical love as love. Then ask clearly for what you need. 'I don't need advice, I just need you to listen.' Mountains can learn that sentence. They just need to hear it, plainly, from someone they trust.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, 'have you eaten' was their way of saying 'I love you.'

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Mu, not every sad message needs a five-step plan.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Mist and mountain. Rare and beautiful. Learn the language.

gi-earth.title: Rain on the garden bed
gi-earth.text: You were the rain and they were the garden bed, and the question was always who controlled the mud. Your Gi Earth ex asked practical questions. 'When will you be home?' 'Did you call them back?' You answered with a feeling, or a song, or nothing. When your mood shifted, they tried to organise it, and you felt managed. They felt you were unreliable; you felt they were controlling. Both of you avoid conflict, so resentments built silently. They'd ask what was wrong; you'd say nothing; both of you would let it sit. Wanting to be understood without explaining, and being asked for explanations constantly, is the knot here. What you miss is being looked out for: someone always checking you got home, that the heating was on, that you'd taken a coat. Answer the actual question, then add your feeling. 'Home at 8. Feeling a bit low.' Clarity and emotion in one line. It's how rain and gardens learn to grow things together.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: 'What's wrong?' 'Nothing.' The most expensive word in your relationship.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, ask 'help or company?' and trust the answer.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gye, answer the question. Then send the poem.

gyeong-metal.title: The sword and the morning dew
gyeong-metal.text: You loved a sword, and it tried very hard to protect you. Your Gyeong Metal ex was strong, direct, and fiercely loyal. But their bluntness cut you more than they knew. They texted the plan for the day like orders; you replied with a photo of the fog, no caption, and they didn't know what to do with it. When they wanted answers now, you needed a day to know your own heart. They became protective, then controlling; you withdrew, then kept things to yourself. There were midnights when they wanted a verdict and you didn't have one yet, and the silence between you felt like a wall. Feeling safe and pressured by the same person is the knot you're still untying. Their loyalty is what you miss. You never doubted they'd fight for you. Answer the actual question first, then share the mood. 'Yes, dinner at 8. Feeling foggy today.' Directness isn't betraying your softness. It gives strong people a way to help you without guessing.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gye, a captionless fog photo is not an answer to 'dinner at 8?'

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gyeong, ask what the photo means. Then wait.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Tough love needs a soft centre. You had one. Use it.

sin-metal.title: Silver in the rain
sin-metal.text: You were the rain on the silver, soft and quiet, and they shone a little more around you. Your Sin Metal ex was refined and sensitive and full of small, precise observations. One of those observations would land on you, and you'd go quiet. They'd read your quiet as coldness, and pull back too. Then you'd be two people in the same flat, both hurt, both silent, both waiting. Neither of you likes conflict, so small hurts collected like water in a gutter. Their critiques stung; your moods confused them. Texts were thoughtful and delayed, and both of you overanalysed every gap. Being loved subtly and missing it, and being missed in return, is the ache. Their elegance is what tugs. They made your gentle world feel refined and chosen, as if your softness were something worth framing rather than fixing. Say 'that hurt' gently and quickly, instead of going quiet. One soft sentence can stop a week of silence before it starts. You don't need the perfect words. You need the first ones.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, 'that hurt' said gently beats a week of quiet.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Sin, your 'small comment' wasn't small to them.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: A late reply is just a late reply. Repeat it.

im-water.title: The ocean and the rain
im-water.text: Same water, different depths. They were the ocean; you were the rain. Your Im Water ex was big, brilliant, restless, the person everyone noticed in a room. You were quieter, deep in a different way. Their restlessness could overwhelm you. Your moods could weigh on them. Both of you dealt with conflict by drifting rather than talking. In groups, they talked over you without noticing, and you noticed every time and didn't say it. You'd start a sentence, they'd finish a different one, and the table would laugh. You felt overshadowed. They had no idea. Feeling small next to someone you loved for being big is the part that lingers. You admired the very thing that drowned you out. The recognition is what tugs. They understood your inner world without needing it explained, and that kind of understanding is rare. Say it the first time. 'I was trying to say something.' It's not rude. It's how you make sure your voice is part of the water, not lost in it.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, your voice matters in the room. Say it the first time.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, you talked over them at every dinner. They counted.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Silence isn't rejection. Still, say something.

gye-water.title: Two raindrops on one window
gye-water.text: Two Gye Waters: tender, dreamy, and a bit lost together. Song links, poems, half-finished thoughts at 2am, a whole playlist made for one rainy Tuesday. It was lovely. Then the hurts came, and you both went inward at once. Both of you avoid decisions. Moods amplified: two sad raindrops make a storm. Practical life got neglected, the bills, the plans, the dull scaffolding that holds a life up, and the fridge was often just oat milk and good intentions. Secrets and silences grew. When both of you were low at the same time, nobody pulled the other out, and a rainy week could turn into a rainy month. You loved each other gently, and gentleness wasn't enough to keep things afloat. The understanding is what pulls you. Nobody else ever felt so much like home in your own private language. Say practical things plainly. 'Rent is due Friday.' 'I need help.' And agree with yourself that a missed reply is never a test. Plain words can be soft too.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Two raindrops. Lovely. Who paid the electricity bill?

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You understood each other so deeply. Keep that, wherever you go.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: A missed reply is never a test. Ever.
